newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Taiwan progresses at WTO but awaits big brother.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan progresses at WTO but awaits big brother.

text.p: Major trading nations on Friday held their first meeting in two years on Taiwan entering the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and cited progress in bilateral negotiations to improve market access, trade officials said.
But Taipei's application to the 130-member watchdog remains inextricably linked to the stalled, 10-year bid by China to join, according to trade sources.
The separate WTO working party negotiating the terms of Beijing's accession meets next Thursday.
Countries welcomed progress on Taiwan but also said they awaited the island, the world's ninth largest trading nation, further bringing domestic legislation into line with WTO rules.
The United States expressed concern over barriers in agricultural, telecom and financial services and said it was seeking more liberalisation in Taiwan's offer, officials said.
Canada was also seeking concessions in agriculture and fish industries and reviewing the services sector, while the European Union was looking at agriculture, according to trade officials.
"Countries are more than satisfied with progress," said one.
"Taiwan would like to end the talks quickly. Of course, it is in their interest," he added.
Sheu Ke-Sheng, vice minister of Economic Affairs, headed the delegation from the customs territory of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen and Matsu to the talks, the first being held under the WTO.

WTO's predecessor body, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), first set up a working party to negotiate "Chinese Taipei's" terms of entry in September 1992. The last formal meeting was in December 1994, a month before WTO succeeded GATT.

China, which has seen Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has said it would accept Taiwan's membership in WTO as a customs territory -- but only after Beijing itself is admitted. Taiwan has completed bilateral talks with eight countries including Australia, Japan and South Korea, but is still talking with partners including the Unitd States, Canada and the EU.
Lee Sands, assistant U.S. Trade Representative, told the closed-door meeting that Washington was very pleased with the state of bilateral talks, according to trade sources.
He welcomed Taiwan intention to join WTO's government procurement pact and awaited its offer in the Information Technology Agreement, they added.

The U.S. expected to hold a new round of bilateral talks with Taiwan in March and would seek further farm liberalisation, specifically trade in pork, poultry and beef products, Sands said. U.S. pork exports faced access problems in Taiwan.
Washington also wanted Taiwan to make offers in telecoms, power supply and transport, according to trade sources.
Taiwan's offer on automobiles should grant equal access to U.S. and EU car manufacturers, they quoted Sands as saying.
The United States expressed pleasure that Taiwan would be dismantling its monopolies in the tobacco and liquor sectors.
No date was set for the next WTO working party meeting on Taiwan, although bilateral negotiations were due to continue.
Sands and other trade officials were staying in Geneva for negotiations with China's delegation led by Long Yongtu, China's main negotiator and an assistant foreign trade minister.
Long is already in Geneva and will hold bilateral negotiations next week ahead of Thursday's formal WTO meeting.
